description: We are computer science students passionate about AI, software development, and solving real-world problems. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we aim to build a climate-resilient crop rotation tool using NASA Earth data to help farmers make informed decisions. We welcome teammates skilled in Python, AI/ML, data science, GIS, agriculture, and UI/UX design. Teamwork, creativity, and a willingness to learn are what matter most!
summary: FieldShift is an intelligent agricultural decision-support platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It uses NASA Earth observations to analyze environmental risks such as heat, drought, soil moisture loss, and erosion, then compares crop rotation strategies to help farmers choose more climate-resilient and sustainable farming plans.
details:
FieldShift is an agricultural decision-support platform created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It combines NASA and Earth observation data—including NASA POWER, SMAP, GPM, Landsat, MODIS/VIIRS, SRTM, USDA SSURGO, and SoilGrids—to identify farm-level risks such as heat stress, drought, soil-moisture deficits, erosion, and declining soil health. Farmers can register fields, view environmental insights on an interactive map, compare baseline, regenerative-soil, and climate/water-resilient crop rotations, and adjust priorities such as water resilience, climate suitability, soil improvement, erosion protection, crop diversity, and market liquidity. The system uses Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis and a Genetic Algorithm to generate biologically feasible multi-season crop plans while enforcing constraints such as crop suitability, water requirements, and disease breaks. It also provides climate-stress simulations, transparent data-provenance cards, and printable decision reports so recommendations support—not replace—farmer and agronomist judgment.

The project’s intended impact is to help farmers adapt to changing climate conditions, conserve water, improve soil health, reduce erosion, protect biodiversity, and strengthen long-term food security. We developed it using Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLite, and asynchronous NASA/data-provider APIs for the backend, with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, and interactive map components for the frontend. Its creativity comes from combining multiple NASA observations with explainable agricultural optimization rather than presenting data as isolated measurements. Our team considered scientific accuracy, uncertainty, data resolution, missing observations, regional differences, farmer priorities, biological crop-rotation rules, usability, privacy, and the need to clearly distinguish live data from calibrated demo data.
